#### What this PR does / why we need it:

This PR adds one test case which exemplifies how a Node addition + Service update while an on-going Node sync is occurring can both add and remove the same node from the load balancer's set of backend nodes. 

The second commit fixes the issue by changing `lastSyncedNodes` to be keyed per service key. This can then be accessed from both the service and node control loops and synchronize the nodes used for any load balancer sync, between both controllers. This also fixes the broken test case added in commit 1.

> @aojea are you OK to followup the test questions? The controller LGTM

yes, let's see if we can make the mock addition optional at least

Let's do a step back, I think that something is odd here, 
1.  This controller react on Nodes and Services
2. The Service logic seems relatively easy
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/16623991318567cd6c29e2114867e7654f25c825/staging/src/k8s.io/cloud-provider/controllers/service/controller.go#L873-L876

3. Nodes are more complex, the worker process nodes and requeue some Services https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/16623991318567cd6c29e2114867e7654f25c825/staging/src/k8s.io/cloud-provider/controllers/service/controller.go#L272-L273

syncNodes reconciles the whole cluster

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/16623991318567cd6c29e2114867e7654f25c825/staging/src/k8s.io/cloud-provider/controllers/service/controller.go#L716-L729

and do that by calling to `updateLoadbalacerHosts` https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/16623991318567cd6c29e2114867e7654f25c825/staging/src/k8s.io/cloud-provider/controllers/service/controller.go#L791-L794

that parallelize `nodeSyncService` for all services

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/16623991318567cd6c29e2114867e7654f25c825/staging/src/k8s.io/cloud-provider/controllers/service/controller.go#L809-L812

that interesting seems to call without actually `lockedUpdateLoadBalancerHosts` holding the lock

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/16623991318567cd6c29e2114867e7654f25c825/staging/src/k8s.io/cloud-provider/controllers/service/controller.go#L749-L754

and this updates the loadbalancer

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/16623991318567cd6c29e2114867e7654f25c825/staging/src/k8s.io/cloud-provider/controllers/service/controller.go#L826-L838

So it seems we have to paths updating loadbalancers, so it will always race, if I create a Service and I update a Node at the same time, both events will follow different paths, no?

If my reasoning is correct the problem of races is not solvable meanwhile there are two independent paths in the controller updating loadbalancer, why don't we have just one place to sync the loadbalancer and the controller on the Node worker checks the impacted Service and just requeue the Service

> If my reasoning is correct the problem of races is not solvable meanwhile there are two independent paths in the controller updating loadbalancer, why don't we have just one place to sync the loadbalancer and the controller on the Node worker checks the impacted Service and just requeue the Service

I _think_ the reason they have seperate paths is because we don't want to block reconciling service updates, because we are stuck processing all services/load balancers from a node update. That might have any changes on the service object (ex adding an annotation) take minutes to process if the controllers are busy processing _any_ node update.

Moreover: my goal here was to fix the problem at hand (possibly also back-port this), so I'd like the implementation to remain as small as possible and avoid refactoring.

> _think_ the reason they have seperate paths is because we don't want to block reconciling service updates, because we are stuck processing all services/load balancers from a node update. That might have any changes on the service object (ex adding an annotation) take minutes to process if the controllers are busy processing _any_ node update.

but why do we want to fix a corner case if the fundamental logic is wrong https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/121091/files#r1373296928

> but why do we want to fix a corner case if the fundamental logic is wrong

I don't know that the logic is wrong. Any node update _needs_ to re-sync all load balancers (so will take a lot of time). Any service update only needs to sync one load balancer. We definitely don't want any service update to wait on the node update to finish cycling through all load balancers before starting, because that will slow down that service update by quite a lot. 

Another idea I had was using a`map[string]sync.Mutex`, where the key is the service key. In that case we could lock the API call, because it would only be locked for that particular service. But the core issue here is really just synchronizing the nodes and making sure that they are always correct and up-to-date when performing the API call

> I don't think this is worse. It still leaves a lot of ??? in there, though.

keep digging and see how you get still more ???? , I only checked the gce cloud provider code and both `UpdateLoadBalancer` and `EnsureLoadBalancer` hold a shared lock for the internal loadbalancers implementation for both Update and Ensure and  only is locked on Ensure for the external loadbalancers

I don't have doubts this is better, I just don't think is ok having two reconcile loops stomping into each other in this very expensive and slow API calls (at least in GCE: forwarding rule, bakends service, firewall rules, target pool or instance groups ...) can be O(minutes) ... we had issues with customers with a considerable number of loadbalancers complaining about the time it takes to sync the loadbalancers

This doesn't make the time to update LBs better or worse I think.  Fundamentally that is limited by the control plane programming time.  Actually this should be better in that you are less likely to end up with a stale set of backends, thus needing toi run again - right?

We can consider rearchitecture - it certainly seems like the code-paths should converge - but I don't think that should block this (unless we really think this is worse :)  It seems like fundamentally we have a queue of "services to update".  When a service changes, enqueue it.  When a node changes, enqueue all services.  Except I sort of buy the argument that updates to specific services should jump the queue.  And maybe deletes should jump the queue.  So we actually have N priority queues which can be processed by M workers.

Current mode of having two loops, one for node and one for service is causing issues downstream on customers and is super complex to troubleshoot, since the implementations details of each cloud provider is an important factor: some operations insde the loadbalancer methods lock, per example in GCE,  causing all the operations to be serialized and since there are 5 workers , in large cluster there can be changes that take more than one hour

If we remove the node loop this is no longer needed, I rather prefer to invest on fixing the root problem

> Actually this should be better in that you are less likely to end up with a stale set of backends, thus needing toi run again - right?

Right, that's the intention. 

> If we remove the node loop this is no longer needed, I rather prefer to invest on fixing the root problem

I don't really follow what the proposal is, are you saying we should stop watching nodes?

I spent some time today talking to Antonio, and I think I understand his point.

This code today is non-obvious and (see my notes above) seems ripe for "fixing".  But the "fixes" are very hard to reason about without also looking into the per-cloud code.  I realized why one path ends up at "ensure" (which has overhead to habdle "create") and another at "update" - because in the case of a node change, we know the service existed AND had a load-balancer, so we don't need to call "ensure".  If we "fix" this, it *might* cause 3x or 4x the number of cloud-provider API calls doing work taht doesn't need to be done.  That will pass e2e but will explode at scale, causing an outage for folks like the GKE, EKS, AKS, etc teams.

Or it might be fine.

So when he says "fixing the root problem" I hear "how would we design this if we were starting over?"  Maybe we would have a single channel, into which we feed service names which need LB updates, and let the cloud-provider code figure out how to parallelize and when to call ensure vs. update.?  But that would be an incompatible change, requiring providers to opt-in.

As to this PR, I don't think it makes that better or worse, but as we "simplify" some parts of this, it makes us question the rest.

@aojea - did I capture it?  Are you OK to proceed with this PR, and we can consider how to fix this properly in a different context?  Or am I still missing it?

issue_context.title: [KCCM]: service update while node sync is processing might impact ingress
issue_context.body:
### What happened?

The Kubernetes cloud controller manager uses resource watchers to sync load balancers, a Node/Service watcher. The Node watcher is slower by nature since any Node event will sync all service load balancers on the cluster. The service watcher is quicker since it only syncs the service load balancer which the event relates to. 

How slow a Node sync is will vary on the cluster, i.e: amount of Services of `type: LoadBalancer` and Nodes, but on big clusters with a lot of churn: the time to process one Node sync can be sufficiently slow to have the cache of Nodes go stale w.r.t the actual cluster state. The cache of Nodes is here the resource informer cache. When syncing Nodes the Node control loop will list all Nodes in its cache and then iterate over all Services and sync their load balancers in parallel, see: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/cloud-provider/controllers/service/controller.go#L799-L818

If any Service experiences an update needing a load balancer sync, the Service controller will also list the Nodes in the informer cache, but retrieve a more up-to-date copy, see: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/cloud-provider/controllers/service/controller.go#L438-L451. 

During upgrades or similar operations where a lot of Nodes get added/deleted: it's rather easy for the following to occur;

1. Node sync is processing, N load balancers are synced
2. NodeY is added
2. Service update triggers sync for load balancer X. It lists and adds NodeY to the load balancer set
3. Node sync processes load balancer Y and removes NodeY from the load balancer set 

This add + remove from the load balancer set might impact ingress SLOs for any application running on NodeY after its creation. 

/sig network
/cc @thockin @aojea 

### What did you expect to happen?

Any node added to the load balancer set which doesn't have a reason (i.e: [predicate](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/cloud-provider/controllers/service/controller.go#L996-L1016)) to be removed should not be removed from the load balancer's set of backend nodes.  

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Update a Service while an upgrade is on-going. Nodes risk being added/removed/added from the load balancer's set of backend nodes at sporadic moments. Alternatively, I have written a unit tests that exhibits the issue and while file a fix PR where this can be seen.  

### Anything else we need to know?
